section_summary: This section documents U.S., British, and Canadian concern over Japanese acquisition of petroleum, ores, metals, rubber, cotton, asbestos, and other strategic commodities, particularly from Latin America and the United States. It includes diplomatic telegrams, procurement-policy memoranda, export-control correspondence, congressional and public protests, commercial intelligence reports, and cross-reference sheets. The papers show Japanese buyers outbidding Allied procurement efforts, exploiting gaps in export controls, and sometimes serving as intermediaries for German requirements.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Lima telegram no. 161 on Japanese purchases in Peru
subfiles.about: Reports persistent Japanese bids for Peruvian minerals and large forward purchases of the 1941 cotton crop.
subfiles.summary: Lima telegram 161: four major mining firms refuse Japanese offers but smaller producers may accept high prices; Japanese cotton contracts cover about a fifth of the crop with substantial financing, calling for U.S. attention.

subfiles.title: Note agreeing to a strategic-material procurement conference
subfiles.about: Agrees with Feis's recommendation and proposes arranging a conference in Jesse Jones's office.
subfiles.summary: Welles supports the recommendation and will join the strategic-material procurement meeting, suggesting Monday or Wednesday next week.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on acquiring Latin American strategic and critical materials
subfiles.about: Reviews the stalled U.S. program to purchase Latin American strategic materials in the face of higher Japanese bids.
subfiles.summary: Feis argues that the program had made little progress beyond copper, Argentine zinc, Brazilian manganese, and Bolivian tin arrangements. He reviews negotiations with Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Argentina, and Mexico, emphasizing that Japanese prices were often much higher and that Latin American governments saw little reason to sacrifice income while the United States still sold oil to Japan. He recommends dedicated interagency purchasing representatives for each major producing country.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary's follow-up note to Feis
subfiles.about: Asks about progress in the struggle over strategic supplies and offers personal assistance.
subfiles.summary: Welles asks Feis how the effort is going and offers to intervene directly if it would help.

subfiles.title: Original Lima telegram no. 161
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese purchases of Peruvian minerals and cotton threaten U.S. control of strategic supplies.
subfiles.summary: Cerro de Pasco, W. R. Grace, the Vanadium Corporation, and Huarón reported persistent Japanese offers but continued to refuse them. Smaller producers might sell, while Japanese buyers had contracted for about 30,000 bales—roughly twenty percent of the cotton crop—and were using dollar exchange for their purchases.

subfiles.title: RFC reply concerning Japanese purchases of Costa Rican ipecac
subfiles.from: S. D. Strauss, Federal Loan Agency
subfiles.about: Declines government action against Japanese purchases of Costa Rican ipecac because the commodity was not considered strategic.
subfiles.summary: Strauss says agencies regarded Costa Rican ipecac as medicinal, not strategic, and the quantities small enough for ordinary trade.

subfiles.title: Steinhardt telegram on rubber from French Indochina
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese-French agreement would send significant French Indochinese rubber to Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: Steinhardt telegram: a reliable source says considerable Indochina rubber will reach Japan and Germany under a Japan-France trade agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Philippine shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram concerning iron ore and other Philippine materials shipped to Japan and possible re-export to Germany.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: increasing iron ore and other materials moving from the Philippines to Japan, possibly re-exported to Germany; see telegram 909 in file 862.24/389.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Argentine minerals shipped to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch about tungsten, vanadium, and beryllium believed destined for German use through Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: T. Hudson-Bell believed Argentine shipments to Japan were meant for Germany; see despatch 2337 in file 862.24/391.

subfiles.title: Drafting memorandum on reply to Senator Byrd
subfiles.about: Recommends narrower language for explaining when export licenses will be refused on national-defense grounds.
subfiles.summary: Drafting memo approves the Byrd reply but objects to "in any way"; proposes saying a shipment is denied when weighing many factors shows it would harm national defense.

subfiles.title: Senator Byrd's transmittal of constituent correspondence
subfiles.about: Requests information enabling him to answer a constituent's complaint about exports useful to Germany and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Byrd forwards correspondence alleging American materials aid military purposes and Germany, and asks for an informed statement.

subfiles.title: James Frantz letter protesting petroleum exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Condemns continued American sales of gasoline and crude oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: James Frantz argues petroleum for Japan aids the Axis against Britain, China and possibly the U.S., and urges Congress to stop it.

subfiles.title: White House release limiting aviation-gasoline exports
subfiles.about: Announces presidential approval of restrictions on aviation-gasoline exports.
subfiles.summary: White House release: on Colonel Maxwell's recommendation aviation gasoline is limited to Western Hemisphere destinations, excepting fuel American companies need elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Proclamation expanding export licensing under the National Defense Act
subfiles.to: United States public and export authorities
subfiles.about: Subjects petroleum products, tetraethyl lead, and iron and steel scrap to export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt invokes section 6 of the July 2, 1940 national-defense act and the earlier proclamation establishing export controls. Beginning August 1, petroleum products, tetraethyl lead, and iron and steel scrap could leave the United States only under license. Sumner Welles countersigned as Acting Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Senator Byrd's letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Byrd's transmittal of James Frantz's complaint about shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State confirms receipt of Byrd's May 7 letter with Frantz's enclosure and promises prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Senator Byrd on petroleum export controls
subfiles.about: Explains the legal controls and licensing policy governing petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Byrd high-octane aviation fuel, aviation lubricating oil and other petroleum products already face licensing for Japan, and applications are denied if they would harm defense; controls are continually adjusted.

subfiles.title: Transfer sheet to defense file
subfiles.about: Records the transfer of item 894.24/1378A to a defense file.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains only an administrative transfer notation. It redirects the record to file 811.20 Defense M/2557A.

subfiles.title: Vice President Wallace letter urging an end to exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges the government to choke off American supplies, particularly oil, to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Vice President Wallace fears exports could be used against the U.S., rejects Dutch East Indies oil as justification, and suggests using priority powers to stop the trade quickly but diplomatically.

subfiles.title: C. L. Harriss letter questioning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States continues supplying Japan despite warnings against appeasement.
subfiles.summary: C. L. Harriss, a campaign supporter, challenges opposing appeasement while sending supplies to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Wallace on petroleum exports
subfiles.about: Assures Wallace that petroleum exports to Japan remain under close consideration.
subfiles.summary: Hull apologizes to Wallace for the delayed reply to his May 10 letter, says officials have long studied the matter, and offers to discuss it.

subfiles.title: Dawes inquiry about oil and scrap exports
subfiles.about: Requests information comparing American exports of oil, scrap iron, and related materials to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Damaged letter from Dawes asks whether reported oil and scrap export figures are correct and whether material might reach Japan or Germany.

subfiles.title: Allen reply directing Dawes to the Department of Commerce
subfiles.about: Declines to provide detailed export statistics and identifies the Department of Commerce as the proper source.
subfiles.summary: Allen acknowledges Dawes's inquiry on exports to Japan and the Soviet Union and refers him to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce for trade details.

subfiles.title: Federal Bureau of Investigation routing page
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice
subfiles.about: A heavily damaged administrative page records the routing of an FBI communication into the State Department file.
subfiles.summary: FBI routing page with heading, filing marks and a damaged form of J. Edgar Hoover's name; subject not recoverable.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Rio quoting intelligence on Japanese shipping
subfiles.about: Transmits confidential reports that Japanese ships might be recalled and were loading Brazilian manganese.
subfiles.summary: Rio instruction quotes intelligence that Casa Tozan warned clients goods may be unavailable after April and Japanese steamers were ordered home before a possible May war; schedules didn't confirm, and ships were loading all available manganese.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese petroleum supplies
subfiles.about: Summarizes the scope and preliminary figures of an Office of Production Management study of Japanese petroleum supplies.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Robinson's study credits Japan preliminarily with 23 million barrels from the U.S., four million from the Netherlands Indies, one million from Mexico, six million elsewhere and three million domestic.

subfiles.title: British Embassy report on Mexican metal shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Provides intercepted details of lead, nickel, molybdenum, mercury, and other materials assembled in Mexico for Japanese shipment.
subfiles.summary: Morris reports plans to buy mercury and consignments to Manzanillo of lead, antimony, aluminum, copper and other metals; Phillips and Kobayashi messages mention about 300 tons via the Yokohama Specie Bank; goods may be U.S.-origin, perhaps for Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Finletter acknowledgment to Morris
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the British Embassy report on lead and other materials shipped from Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Finletter thanks Morris for his April 21 letter on lead and other shipments from Mexico to Japan.

subfiles.title: Dent cover letter on copper shipped through Colón
subfiles.about: Forwards a delayed report from the British vice-consul at Colón concerning a copper shipment.
subfiles.summary: Dent sends information telegraphed from Colon on February 17 that arrived late; he doubts it adds to Yost's information and asks about developments.

subfiles.title: Shipping note on copper routed through Colón and New York
subfiles.about: Describes successive copper shipments whose declared routing and consignees changed before departure.
subfiles.summary: Four hundred seventy tons of copper were to go from Colon to Jamaica, with smaller lots after; destination changed from Brazil to New York, and other shipments were reportedly in transit to Osaka.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Mitsubishi petroleum storage at Qingdao
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Quotes W. H. Pinckard's report on Mitsubishi tank construction and imported petroleum at Qingdao.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi completed or began several Qingdao tanks, one for naval use; American gasoline arrives in large drum cargoes, and Japanese firms are holding China stock as military reserves.

subfiles.title: Exton referral note on the Rockhill tin-reclamation letter
subfiles.about: Forwards the Rockhill letter and suggests possible consultation with the War Production Board.
subfiles.summary: Exton identifies the Rockhill tin-reclamation letter discussed with Mr. Bloom January 31 and suggests consulting the War Production Board.

subfiles.title: Rockhill offer of a tin-reclamation process
subfiles.about: Offers the government free access to a process for reclaiming tin strips from discarded cans.
subfiles.summary: Rockhill says his plant recovered tin from institutional cans, about 100 tons monthly including for Japan, until export limits closed it; despite losses he offers his expertise free if reclamation becomes necessary.

subfiles.title: Allen acknowledgment of Rockhill's offer
subfiles.about: Thanks Rockhill and reports forwarding his proposal to appropriate government authorities.
subfiles.summary: Allen summarizes Rockhill's experience and offer to share his process freely, thanks him, and says copies went to relevant agencies.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Rockhill correspondence to the Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.about: Forwards Rockhill's letter and the Department's reply for information.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum sends the Export Control Administrator Rockhill's tin-strip reclamation process; copies also went to the Secretary of War.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Rockhill correspondence to the Secretary of War
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Sends Rockhill's tin-reclamation proposal and the State Department reply to the War Department.
subfiles.summary: State forwards the Rockhill correspondence to Stimson for information; the Export Control Administrator also received copies.

subfiles.title: Dent cover letter forwarding Rockefeller Committee notes
subfiles.about: Forwards copies of intelligence notes recently supplied to the Rockefeller Committee.
subfiles.summary: Dent says Thorold asked him to send Feis notes on Japanese and German acquisition of strategic commodities and other commercial intelligence.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese purchases of Chilean manganese ore
subfiles.about: Describes a Chilean government program buying manganese from small miners for resale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chile's Corporacion del Fomento, via engineer Enrique Vial's department, contracted to sell Japan 5,000 tons of manganese ore and had acquired 3,500; its lower grade threshold attracted miners unable to meet Grace's U.S. specifications.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese purchase of lead vanadate at Tampico
subfiles.about: Reports the sale to Japanese buyers of 200 tons of lead vanadate stored at Tampico.
subfiles.summary: Lead vanadate at Tampico, the final part of purchases under a German company's contract with American Smelting & Refining, was reliably reported sold to Japanese buyers.

subfiles.title: Source report on Brazilian stones, skins, and German destinations
subfiles.about: Summarizes correspondence about Brazilian skins and industrial diamonds purchased with Japanese advance credits.
subfiles.summary: A Bahia trader said Japan began buying better goods with advance payment, apparently for Germany, provoking British seizures; Gustavo in Rio filled a Tokyo order for industrial diamonds.

subfiles.title: Weekly note on a rubber shipment from Pará to Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports financing and shipment of 150 tons of rubber from Pará to Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Rasmoimport opened a $5,000 freight credit December 29 for rubber from Van Mastwyk to ship from Para to Kobe on the Seya Maru.

subfiles.title: Weekly report on German rubber stocks and Brazilian purchases
subfiles.about: Assesses German rubber shortages and reported German purchases in Brazil routed through Japan.
subfiles.summary: German rubber stocks were reportedly low; Germany negotiated about three million dollars of Brazilian rubber, one-third sent through Japan, and proposed making specialized tires for Romania in return for raw rubber.

subfiles.title: Damaged January trade-intelligence report
subfiles.about: A severely degraded report records trade, shipment, and financial information that is largely unrecoverable.
subfiles.summary: Damaged January trade-intelligence report with scattered references to banks, London, shipments and amounts.

subfiles.title: Weekly report on Argentine and Uruguayan wool markets
subfiles.about: Reports continued Soviet and Japanese purchasing activity in South American wool markets.
subfiles.summary: Nilssen, Olsen & Company report unchanged Argentine and Uruguayan wool conditions; Russia buys medium and fine wool and Japan seeks fine wool.

subfiles.title: Report on German propaganda for South America via Siberia
subfiles.about: Describes German-language and Spanish-language propaganda intended for South American circulation.
subfiles.summary: German propaganda for South America via Siberia accuses British forces of attacks on civilians, churches and hospitals, and a Berlin compilation prefaced by von Ribbentrop blames Britain for the war.

subfiles.title: Mixed commercial-intelligence report for early March 1941
subfiles.about: Summarizes intercepted trade and financial communications involving Europe and the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Early March 1941 mixed report: Mexican fluorspar and mercury for Japan, Lisbon currency transfers, Swedish and Canadian pulp competition, Brazilian tobacco and cellulose, and a Mexican permit for importing automatic pistols.

subfiles.title: Trade-intelligence report for February 17–23, with duplicate
subfiles.about: Reports transactions in coffee, metals, rubber, vegetable oil, ixtle, and German films.
subfiles.summary: February 17-23 report: Mexico City aluminum, steel and rubber deals, Sao Paulo cottonseed oil to Stockholm, planned Japanese shipments of Mexican ixtle, and a Berlin request to send Nazi films via New York. Page 516 duplicates it.

subfiles.title: Damaged report on shipments from Brazil and other markets
subfiles.about: A damaged weekly report concerns Brazilian shipments and transit trade involving Japan.
subfiles.summary: Damaged report mentioning a Hamburg correspondent, a Brazilian firm and transit shipment to Japan; details unrecoverable.

subfiles.title: Source extract concerning an invoice to Josef Sprung
subfiles.about: Records a Rio de Janeiro communication to Josef Sprung in Minneapolis concerning an invoice.
subfiles.summary: Extract on an invoice to Josef Sprung, filed under industrial diamonds; commodity description illegible.

subfiles.title: Damaged source extract on boart, castor seeds, and rock crystal
subfiles.about: A largely illegible extract was filed under boart, castor seeds, and rock crystal.
subfiles.summary: Damaged extract on boart, castor seeds and rock crystal; only the date and fragments of a Rio de Janeiro address are dependable.

subfiles.title: Report on Brazilian industrial-diamond routes to Switzerland and Germany
subfiles.about: Describes attempts to move Brazilian industrial diamonds to Switzerland despite British shipping controls.
subfiles.summary: Anton Smit & Company tells Maag Zahnraeder British navicert rules make Brazilian diamond shipments risky; routes considered include via New York, via Japan and Russia, and via Italy, with intervention sought in Berlin for diamonds at Antwerp.

subfiles.title: Political intelligence on Latin American leftist organizations
subfiles.about: Discusses financing, party organization, propaganda, and Popular Front strategy in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Damaged intelligence on Latin American leftist groups in Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Cuba, citing organizational and financial problems and urging coordinated propaganda and Popular Front tactics; many names obscured.

subfiles.title: Feis acknowledgment of Dent's intelligence notes
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the British Embassy's notes on raw-material and related questions.
subfiles.summary: Feis thanks Dent for the copies sent with his April 1 letter; the Department is considering the matters raised.

subfiles.title: Sabath letter urging an end to petroleum shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a manufacturer's complaint about a loophole in export controls and again urges stopping oil and gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sabath says avaricious exporters exploit a legal loophole at the nation's expense and asks Hull to stop petroleum shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: P.M. clipping reproducing a concealed petroleum order for Japan
subfiles.from: P.M. newspaper; Standard-Vacuum Oil Company order
subfiles.about: Reproduces an order for 255,200 gallons of motor oil in 5,200 wooden barrels for shipment to Japan without company branding.
subfiles.summary: P.M. clipping reproduces an order for Pennsylvania motor oil to Moji and Yokohama on the Tusima Maru in wooden barrels with the Socony name removed, read as concealing continued oil exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Myers letter on the wooden-barrel loophole
subfiles.about: Argues that restrictions on steel petroleum drums were being defeated by exports in wooden barrels.
subfiles.summary: Myers says Executive Order 8669 restricted small steel drums but not wooden barrels, so thousands of barrels go to Japan from Gulf ports with steel hoops; he urges extending the restriction to wooden barrels or lifting it.

subfiles.title: Hull acknowledgment to Sabath
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Myers complaint and promises corrective action if exporters are evading existing restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the problem is under careful study and the government will act if exporters defeat the restrictions.

subfiles.title: Canadian Legation letter on asbestos controls
subfiles.about: Explains Canadian asbestos quotas for Japan and requests closer coordination with U.S. export controls.
subfiles.summary: Canada refuses permits for top crude asbestos grades and quotas lower groups; its Metals Controller fears Japanese buyers evade quotas via U.S. re-export, and asks continuing information on U.S. permit policy.

subfiles.title: Secret Canadian memorandum on 1941 asbestos quotas
subfiles.about: Provides confidential details of Canadian asbestos quotas for shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Secret Canadian memo: most grades above Group 5 are limited to half the 1934-1938 average, Group 5 capped at 24,000 tons, with quotas allocated by historical shares; January allowances were about 91 tons of Group 3 and 1,600 of Group 5.

subfiles.title: Green reply on aligning U.S. and Canadian asbestos controls
subfiles.about: Reports new American asbestos controls and welcomes cooperation with Canada.
subfiles.summary: Green says after April 15 asbestos of fibers at least three-eighths inch long comes under U.S. export control, aligning with Canada and hindering quota evasion, and reciprocates Canada's request for administrative cooperation.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum report on Japanese petroleum purchases from the Pacific Coast
subfiles.about: Supplies detailed intelligence on Japanese gasoline, crude-oil, distillate, and lubricating-oil purchases and shipments.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum report: bulk gasoline on the Akatuki Maru and Nitiei Maru, March shipments to Japan about 47,000 barrels daily, 31 tankers possibly loading in May, and Mitsubishi moving barrels to California before an April 15 deadline.
